source: Jagadish et al. (2024) Human-like category learning by injecting ecological priors from LLMs into neural networks
finding: A transformer meta-trained on LLM-generated category tasks (ERMI) explains human data better than seven cognitive models, including the rational model of categorization (RMC).
numbers: Badham 2017 types 1-4, posterior model frequency: ERMI 0.43+-0.05, RMC 0.41+-0.05, MI 0.10, PFN 0.05, GCM/PM/Rule/Rulex <=0.01. Devraj 2021: ERMI 0.32+-0.06, GCM 0.24+-0.05, Rule 0.20+-0.05.
limits: RMC nearly ties ERMI on Badham, so the data barely separate a Bayesian clustering model from the meta-learned one. Participant N not reported in the text read. Only two human datasets.
agent_relevance: Bayesian clustering (RMC) is still a top human-like account; an LLM can supply the prior over tasks instead of hand-built priors.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) Human-like category learning by injecting ecological priors from LLMs into neural networks
finding: ERMI reproduces the Shepard 1961 difficulty order and is far closer to humans than the same network without LLM priors.
numbers: Human error after 15 blocks: type 2 3.2%, type 3 6.1%, type 4 6.5%, type 5 7.5%, type 6 about 10.6%; type 1 zero after 4 blocks. Shepard-fit MSE: ERMI 0.03 vs MI 0.26.
limits: ERMI learns faster than people: it plateaus after about 4 blocks while humans keep improving.
agent_relevance: Ecological priors (which rules are common in the world) matter more than model class for matching human rule difficulty.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) Human-like category learning by injecting ecological priors from LLMs into neural networks
finding: Claude-v2 itself, run directly on the category tasks, matches human choices worse than ERMI distilled from its task samples.
numbers: BIC Badham: ERMI 38722.13 vs Claude-v2 39816.90. Devraj: 41207.20 vs 42401.42 (lower is better). Error MSE vs humans 0.18 (Claude) vs 0.05 (ERMI).
limits: One LLM, one prompt style, temperature 1. Large BIC gaps but only two datasets.
agent_relevance: Using the LLM as a source of priors and tasks beat asking it to categorise directly; relevant to S2 where the model proposes rules.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) Human-like category learning by injecting ecological priors from LLMs into neural networks
finding: The LLM-prior model gives top benchmark accuracy on real tabular classification, so human-like priors do not cost accuracy in ordinary few-shot rule learning.
numbers: 23 OpenML-CC18 tasks, 30 train / 70 test points, 4 features: ERMI 70.95%+-0.54, mean rank 2.26, exceedance probability 0.66; TabPFN 70.51% (0.24); XGBoost rank 2.61.
limits: Two classes and at most 100 features only. Gain over TabPFN is 0.44 points.
agent_relevance: Small but real sign that human-like priors are not a handicap.

source: Jagadish et al. (2024) Human-like category learning by injecting ecological priors from LLMs into neural networks
finding: Generation recipe: a two-stage prompt asked the LLM to invent experiments, then stimuli with labels; most outputs parsed.
numbers: 250 experiments per stage-1 prompt; 100 stimuli with 3 features per task; about 95% parsed; 23,421/20,690/13,693 feature-label sets and 11,518/8,950/12,911 task sets (3/4/6 features). 6-layer transformer, 500,000 episodes.
limits: Fidelity of LLM tasks to real-world statistics is assumed, validated only by fit to human data.
agent_relevance: A scaffold could ask the model to imagine many similar tasks before choosing a rule.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) Human-like few-shot learning via Bayesian reasoning over natural language
finding: An LLM that proposes natural-language hypotheses, weighted by Bayes with a prior tuned to human judgments, models human concept learning (number game, logical concepts).
numbers: Logical concepts (human data: 112 concepts, 1,596 participants): model R2 = .81 with 100 proposals per batch, within 3% of human accuracy, better than GPT-4 alone and better than a classic Bayesian program learner even with a huge sampling budget.
limits: Prior tuning was critical for logical concepts; the untuned pretrained prior was syntax sensitive. Variance across human groups limits the ceiling.
agent_relevance: Direct model of S2: propose a few rules in words, score each against the examples (S7). 50-100 proposals sufficed.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) Human-like few-shot learning via Bayesian reasoning over natural language
finding: On the Number Game, 50-100 sampled hypotheses gave a close fit to the averaged ratings of 8 humans, where the original model used over 5000 hypotheses.
numbers: Python-coded hypotheses fit significantly worse than English ones; removing the data-conditioned proposal gave a poor fit; GPT-4's own ratings differed from humans.
limits: Eight raters only; no ground truth for ambiguous cases like 30 vs 60.
agent_relevance: Natural language is the better hypothesis format for matching human generalisation; condition proposals on the examples.

source: Wong, Grand, Lew, Goodman, Mansinghka, Andreas, Tenenbaum (2023) Human-like few-shot learning via Bayesian reasoning over natural language
finding: New participants learned a majority-colour concept after 2 batches, as the model predicted. Minority colour: model 4 batches, humans 3.
numbers: N = 16 new participants; 2 new concepts.
limits: Tiny out-of-sample test.
agent_relevance: Model errors are inspectable because hypotheses are verbal.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning
finding: Online Bayesian updating over LLM-proposed rules beats batch and refine-only methods on Zendo and ActiveACRE.
numbers: Zendo predictive accuracy out of 8: ReAct LLM 4.60, batch fuzzy 5.35, batch hard 6.55 (best); humans 5.26. ActiveACRE task solving: online hard 0.35 vs batch hard 0.15 and batch-with-refinement 0.10.
limits: Table parsed from PDF text; some Zendo rows may be shifted, check before citing a single cell. One LLM.
agent_relevance: Update the set of candidate rules after each new example (S7); do not generate once.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning
finding: Humans are better fitted by fuzzy, probabilistic rules than by hard rules, even though hard rules score higher accuracy.
numbers: Variance of human accuracy explained: online fuzzy R2 = .57; hard rules R2 = .10; batch R2 = .05; LLM-only ReAct R2 = .25. Log-likelihood of human data: online fuzzy -1478.82, earlier best model -1539, online hard -5209.93.
limits: Zendo rules from Bramley et al.; 10 rules. Per-judgment fit only R2 = .35.
agent_relevance: Keep rules soft with a confidence when checking whether they still fit.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning
finding: Humans and the model both learn a rule outside the designed formal language (majority of blocks red) at a 30-40% rate.
numbers: 30%-40% success for humans and model on the new rule.
limits: New human sample, size not extracted.
agent_relevance: Fixed rule grammars miss human concepts; allow free-text hypotheses.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning capabilities of language models with hypothesis refinement
finding: Iterative hypothesis refinement with a code interpreter lifts GPT-4 rule induction over plain prompting on ACRE, MiniSCAN and List Functions, but not on MiniARC raw accuracy.
numbers: Raw accuracy ACRE: IO 64.0, self-refine 70.0, refinement T=1,N=1 78.2, N=5 79.8. Task accuracy ACRE: IO 28.0 vs 45-48. MiniSCAN task accuracy: IO 0.0 vs 46.0 (T=3,N=1). MiniARC raw: IO 33.1 vs 5.9-12.8.
limits: Text-only model on grid tasks; interpreter is symbolic.
agent_relevance: Verify proposed rules by running them on the examples.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning capabilities of language models with hypothesis refinement
finding: The model proposes good rules but cannot apply them itself: using the LM as interpreter collapses task accuracy.
numbers: MiniSCAN task accuracy falls from over 80% with a symbolic interpreter to almost zero with the LM as interpreter.
limits: Authors note an LM is not expected to match a symbolic interpreter.
agent_relevance: Do not let the same model silently apply its own rule; execute or check it separately.

source: Qiu et al. (2024) Phenomenal yet puzzling: testing inductive reasoning capabilities of language models with hypothesis refinement
finding: Rule induction is brittle to noisy examples and to unfamiliar output vocabulary.
numbers: Perturbing 12.5%, 25%, 50% of 8 exemplars: performance drops even with one noisy example; telling the model to expect noise helps only partly. Pseudoword outputs lower accuracy.
limits: Human comparison was only partial per the authors.
agent_relevance: The rule-fit check (S7) needs outlier tolerance; humans handle some noise.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis search: inductive reasoning with language models
finding: Abstract hypotheses in words, then programs, then verification on examples, beat direct prompting on ARC.
numbers: Random 100 ARC tasks, top-1: direct 17%; hypotheses-to-program 23%; with LLM-summarised hypotheses 30%; human-selected hypotheses 33%; human-written LARC hypotheses 45%. Of 49 tasks with a correct selected hypothesis, 33 (67%) gave correct programs.
limits: GPT-4, 100-task subset. Summarised hypotheses were often vague.
agent_relevance: The 30% to 45% gap shows hypothesis quality is the bottleneck, which supports a better S2 rule-writing step.

source: Lampinen et al. (2022) Can language models learn from explanations in context?
finding: Explanations attached to few-shot examples improve a 280B model and beat matched control text. Closest LLM analogue of explanation-based learning.
numbers: 40 tasks. Untuned explanation gain about one third of the gain from adding few-shot examples and twice the gain from task instructions. Tuned explanations, and picking examples together with explanations, gave larger gains.
limits: Only the largest model benefits. Hand-tuning needs a validation set.
agent_relevance: Store why an example is in a class, not just the label (the EBL idea).

source: MacLellan, Singaravadivelan, Lian, Wang, Langley (2026) A rational account of categorization based on information theory
finding: A Cobweb-based information-theoretic model fits Medin and Schaffer 1978 Exp 1 slightly better than Anderson's RMC.
numbers: Spearman 0.95 vs 0.91 (RMC); Exp 2 predictions nearly identical to the context model.
limits: Aggregated human data only; no ablations yet; preprint.
agent_relevance: Hierarchical (taxonomic) clusters, not flat ones, may be the better structure.

source: MacLellan, Singaravadivelan, Lian, Wang, Langley (2026) A rational account of categorization based on information theory
finding: Reproduces the prototype-to-exemplar shift of Smith and Minda 1998 only when the prior-strength parameter is set high.
numbers: Human: 16 participants, 14 six-letter words, 40 blocks (560 trials); exceptions miscategorised in first 3 of 10 segments, improve from segment 4. Model: alpha = 2 gives the phase change; alpha < 0.6 classifies exceptions right from segment 1; alpha = 1 resembles HDP.
limits: Parameters set by hand, no guessing parameter, qualitative only.
agent_relevance: Early on use a broad rule or prototype, later memorise exceptions; one dial (prior strength) controls it.

source: Gershman and Blei (2012) A tutorial on Bayesian nonparametric models
finding: Anderson's rational model is the Chinese-restaurant-process mixture, a Dirichlet process model that learns the number of categories; later work extended it.
numbers: Cited extensions: Griffiths et al. 2007, Heller et al. 2009, Sanborn et al. 2010.
limits: Tutorial; no new human data.
agent_relevance: The number of rules is not fixed in advance; let evidence create a new one.

source: Wikipedia: Explanation-based learning
finding: EBL needs a strong domain theory, learns from one example by proving it, and suffers the utility problem (Minton 1990).
numbers: Years cited: Minton 1990, Samuelsson and Rayner 1991, Mitchell textbook 1997.
limits: Encyclopedic summary, not Mitchell, Keller and Kedar-Cabelli 1986 itself.
agent_relevance: Only works when the agent has a reliable theory; otherwise one case yields a wrong rule.

source: Lee, Wills, Schlegelmilch (2026) Is generalization general? Differences between predictive and category learning
finding: Generalisation gradients differ by test format and framing, much less by whether the task is category or prediction learning.
numbers: Exp 1 N = 277 analysed (of 309); Exp 2 N = 245 (of 348). Decisions gave steeper gradients (BF > 1000). Absolute framing gave about 20% more Gaussian gradients (BF > 1000). Domain slope BF = 6.5; domain interactions (BF 47.5, 5.1) did not replicate in the second test phase.
limits: The light/dark dimension may have encouraged rule-like responding; no clustering model was fitted.
agent_relevance: Test wording changes generalisation; keep the test format fixed when checking rules.

source: Kumar, Dasgupta, Daw, Cohen, Griffiths (2022) Disentangling abstraction from statistical pattern matching
finding: Humans do better on tasks built from abstract rules than on statistics-matched metamer tasks; neural networks show the reverse.
numbers: Networks beat humans on metamer tasks in 7 of 8 abstractions; one test t(518) = -0.953, p = .341.
limits: Only skimmed for numbers; grid-board task.
agent_relevance: A good test for whether a system holds a rule or only a pattern.

source: Poth (2023) Probabilistic learning and psychological similarity
finding: Philosophical review: Bayesian concept learning needs a similarity-space reading of its probabilities; Shepard's law ties generalisation to exponential decay with dissimilarity.
numbers: No new data.
limits: Opinion review.
agent_relevance: Priors in a Bayesian rule learner should rest on a similarity notion the agent can state.

source: Anderson (1991) The adaptive nature of human categorization
finding: Recalled, not read: rational model; a category is a cluster, chosen by a prior favouring larger clusters times feature likelihood; a new cluster is created when nothing fits. Fits Medin-Schaffer 1978 and Hayes-Roth 1977 data (also confirmed second-hand in b17).
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Original is serial and order dependent.
agent_relevance: S2/S7: add a new rule when no old one fits.

source: Love, Medin, Gureckis (2004) SUSTAIN: a network model of category learning
finding: Recalled, not read: starts with one cluster, adds a cluster only on a surprising error, attention weights focus on useful features; fits Shepard types and inference versus classification.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: From memory; verify mismatches before relying on it.
agent_relevance: Add rules only after a surprise, not eagerly.

source: Sanborn, Griffiths, Navarro (2010) Rational approximations to rational models
finding: Recalled, not read: particle-filter versions of Anderson's model with few particles capture human order effects and individual differences.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: From memory only.
agent_relevance: Few sampled hypotheses can be enough, as in b06-b08.

source: Mitchell, Keller, Kedar-Cabelli (1986) Explanation-based generalization: a unifying view
finding: Recalled, not read: EBG generalises one example by explaining it with a domain theory and keeping only the features the proof uses.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: Needs a correct, complete theory.
agent_relevance: A rule from one example is safe only when the explanation is checked.

source: Tenenbaum (1999) Bayesian modeling of human concept learning; Tenenbaum and Griffiths (2001)
finding: Recalled, not read: size principle, so smaller consistent hypotheses get higher likelihood and few positive examples narrow the concept; fits number game and rectangle learning.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: From memory only.
agent_relevance: Prefer the tightest rule that fits all examples.

source: Pazzani (1991) Influence of prior knowledge on concept acquisition
finding: Recalled, not read: prior knowledge changes which concepts are easy, in a way explanation-based models predict.
numbers: Not read this session.
limits: From memory only; verify.
agent_relevance: Background knowledge can help or mislead.
